paragraphs.text: Space Shuttle Columbia broke apart during re-entry.
But that was only the visible part. Space Shuttle Columbia broke apart during re-entry. The key figure: 7 CREW.

To see why, look at the structure itself. Jan 16, 2003: Launch; foam strike on the left wing. Feb 1, 2003: Break-up during re-entry over Texas. Space Shuttle Columbia broke apart as it came home. All seven astronauts were killed minutes before landing. The damage happened sixteen days earlier, at launch. A piece of insulating foam hit the left wing. It punched a hole in the heat shield panel. On re-entry, superheated gas poured into the wing. The structure melted from the inside. After that, every shuttle's heat shield was inspected in orbit.
And the warning signs were already there. The mechanism: foam strike breaching a reinforced carbon-carbon panel on the wing's leading edge.

Then the chain began. The trigger: a suitcase-sized piece of foam hitting the left wing at launch. Foam had hit shuttles on earlier flights, so it came to be treated as routine. That normalization is why the damage was never checked in orbit.

This is the moment it could no longer be stopped. Step 1 of the failure chain: foam breaks off external tank. Step 2 of the failure chain: strikes left wing leading edge. Step 3 of the failure chain: hole in heat shield panel. Step 4 of the failure chain: hot gas enters wing on re-entry. Step 5 of the failure chain: orbiter breaks apart.
Which leaves one question. What changed: shuttles were inspected in orbit for heat-shield damage on every later flight.
But that was only the visible part. Engineers asked for satellite images of the wing and were turned down. What should happen when a warning is inconvenient?

miniNarrative: The Space Shuttle was a partially reusable spacecraft operated by the US National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA).
It flew in space for the first time in April 1981, and was used to conduct in-orbit research, and deploy commercial, military, and scientific payloads.
At launch, it consisted of the orbiter, which contained the crew and payload, the external tank (ET), and the two solid rocket boosters (SRBs).
The orbiter was a reusable, winged vehicle that launched vertically and landed as a glider.
shorts.payoff: Debris was reported from east Texas through southern Louisiana.
